**Slides covered.** `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 4-69; `BIOS-767-Part-014.pdf`, slides 4-43; `BIOS-767-Part-015.pdf`, slide 17.

## Motivation

A GLM specifies the response distribution, linear predictor, and link. It is the mean-model building block for GEE and GLMM. A pooled GLM does not by itself account for repeated-measure dependence.

## Exponential-family formulation

For independent $Y_i$,

$$
f(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)=
\exp\left\{
\frac{w_i\{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)\}}{\phi}
+c(y_i,\phi,w_i)
\right\}.
$$

Then

$$
\mu_i=E(Y_i)=b'(\theta_i),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{\phi}{w_i}b''(\theta_i)
=\frac{\phi}{w_i}v(\mu_i).
$$

The systematic component is

$$
\eta_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta,\qquad
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i,\qquad
\mu_i=g^{-1}(x_i^\mathsf T\beta).
$$

If $g(\mu_i)=\theta_i$, the link is canonical. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 16-35.*

## Core outcome models

### Binary

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),\qquad
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=x_i^\mathsf T\beta.
$$

For a one-unit increase in $x_k$, holding other covariates fixed,

$$
\frac{\operatorname{odds}(Y=1\mid x_k+1)}
{\operatorname{odds}(Y=1\mid x_k)}
=e^{\beta_k}.
$$

### Count and rate

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),\qquad
\log\mu_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta+\log e_i,
$$

where $e_i$ is exposure. Therefore $e^{\beta_k}$ is a rate ratio. The Poisson condition $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i$ may be relaxed through quasi-Poisson $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i$ or a negative-binomial mean-variance relation. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 20-35 and 66-69.*

### Gaussian

$$
Y_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2),\qquad
\mu_i=x_i^\mathsf T\beta.
$$

This is the identity-link special case.

## Estimation

The score can be written

$$
U(\beta)=
\sum_i
\left(\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\beta}\right)^\mathsf T
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)^{-1}(Y_i-\mu_i).
$$

For the canonical link this is proportional to $\sum_i x_i(Y_i-\mu_i)$. Newton-Raphson/Fisher scoring yields iteratively reweighted least squares. The asymptotic covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta)\approx
\left[
\sum_i
\left(\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\beta}\right)^\mathsf T
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)^{-1}
\left(\frac{\partial\mu_i}{\partial\beta}\right)
\right]^{-1}.
$$

*Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 36-43. The score derivation is on slides 37-41.*

## Deviance and inference

The residual deviance compares the fitted model with the saturated model:

$$
D(y;\widehat\mu)=
2\{\ell(y;y,\widehat\phi)-\ell(\widehat\mu;y,\widehat\phi)\}.
$$

For nested $M_0\subset M_1$ with known dispersion,

$$
D_0-D_1=2(\ell_1-\ell_0)
\ \dot\sim\ \chi_{p_1-p_0}^2.
$$

The difference-of-deviance approximation is generally more reliable than treating a single residual deviance as $\chi^2_{N-p}$. Wald inference uses the estimated information. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 44-64.*

The Pearson dispersion statistic is

$$
\widehat\phi_P=
\frac{\sum_i(Y_i-\widehat\mu_i)^2/v(\widehat\mu_i)}{N-p}.
$$

Large values under Poisson/binomial sampling indicate overdispersion, but can also reflect a misspecified mean, omitted dependence, zero inflation, or outliers.

## Quasi-likelihood

If only $E(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi v(\mu_i)$ are specified, solve the same quasi-score $U(\beta)=0$. The resulting estimator does not require a full outcome distribution, but likelihood quantities such as AIC and ordinary LRTs are unavailable. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-013.pdf`, slides 66-69.*

## Longitudinal interpretation

A pooled GLM coefficient has the intended mean-model interpretation but an independence-based standard error is generally invalid for repeated outcomes. Embed the mean model in:

- GEE for population-averaged effects;
- GLMM for subject-specific effects;
- a transition model for effects conditional on response history.

With nonlinear links, these parameters are not interchangeable. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-014.pdf`, slides 10-43.*

## When to apply

Use a GLM directly for independent responses or as a benchmark. For clustered outcomes, use cluster-robust covariance only when the number of independent clusters is adequate, or use a longitudinal model that explicitly addresses association.
